title.en: King Jeongjo's Diary of Daily Reflection

summaryEn: As a young royal heir, Jeongjo kept a diary to look back on each day. It grew into the Ilseongnok, an official record of the court from 1760 to 1910.
learningGoalsEn: Know that the 일성록 (Ilseongnok) began from Jeongjo's personal diary, kept when he was the royal grandson and heir, 세손 (seson).
Know that Jeongjo was moved by Zengzi's words in the Analects about looking back on oneself every day, and kept a diary to reflect.
Know that from 1783 it became an official court record written by Gyujanggak officials, with headlines and details for easy reading.
Read and understand 오늘 (oneul), 반성 (banseong), 일기를 써요 (ilgireul sseoyo) and 오늘 하루를 돌아봐요 (oneul harureul dorabwayo).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya opens an old book about a young royal heir named Jeongjo. As the king's grandson who would one day be king, he was called {kw:seson}. Even then, he kept a diary of what he said, did and studied.
scenes.artBrief: A young royal heir in plain traditional clothes writing in a small book at a low desk by lamplight; Hoya reading a book about him in the foreground.

art.altEn: A young royal heir writes his diary at a low desk by lamplight, while Hoya reads a book about him.

scenes.narrationEn: Why? One reason was the words of Zengzi in an old book, the Analects, about looking back on yourself every day. Jeongjo was deeply moved by them and wanted to look back on himself, too.
scenes.captionEn: Words about looking back each day
scenes.artBrief: The prince pausing with brush raised, looking thoughtfully out of a window at an evening sky.

art.altEn: The young prince pauses with his brush raised and gazes out of the window at the evening sky, thinking.

scenes.narrationEn: His diary was called the Jonhyeongak Diary. After Jeongjo became king, he kept writing it himself. Hoya tries it too and asks, 'What did I do today?'
scenes.captionEn: Hoya asks, 'What did I do today?'
scenes.artBrief: Split scene: King Jeongjo in royal dress writing at night; Hoya in his den with a tiny notebook, scratching his head.

art.altEn: King Jeongjo writes his diary by lamplight, and Hoya, trying it too, wonders what he did today.

scenes.narrationEn: As state business grew, Jeongjo had too much to write himself. So in 1783, officials of the royal library, Gyujanggak, began writing the diary about state affairs and gave it to the king to approve. His personal diary became an official record.
scenes.artBrief: Scholars at the Gyujanggak library writing at desks, then presenting a bound book to the king, who reads it carefully.

art.altEn: A royal library scholar writes the diary at a desk, and an official presents the bound book to the king to approve.

scenes.narrationEn: UNESCO translates its title, {kw:ilseongnok}, as 'Records of Daily Reflections.' Each entry starts with a short headline, and the details follow, which made it easy to read.
scenes.artBrief: An open book page drawn with one bold line of strokes at top and smaller lines below (no readable text), a finger tracing the bold line.

art.altEn: An open diary page starts each entry with one bold headline line, with smaller lines of detail after it.

scenes.narrationEn: The {kw:ilseongnok} looks like a diary written from the king's point of view, but it was really an official government record. Today, 2,329 books covering 1760 to 1910 are kept at Seoul National University's Gyujanggak.
scenes.captionEn: A diary that is an official record
scenes.artBrief: A modern library stack with rows of old thread-bound books in protective cases, a curator in gloves checking one.

art.altEn: In a modern archive, a curator in a white coat checks one of the old thread-bound books kept in protective boxes.

scenes.narrationEn: The {kw:ilseongnok} is a National Treasure, and in 2011 UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World. Hoya decides to write one line tonight: what went well today, and what to do better.
scenes.captionEn: Hoya looks back on the day
scenes.artBrief: Hoya at night writing in a notebook by a small lamp, a crescent moon in the window, smiling.

art.altEn: At night Hoya sits by a small lamp with his notebook, a crescent moon in the window, and writes one line about his day.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. All Sillok entries (Taejong 4/2/8 #4; Jeongjo 19/leap2/13 #1 and #3) re-fetched from sillok.history.go.kr and compared to original Chinese/Korean text. Every non-UNESCO URL cited was re-fetched fresh and every quote segment machine-matched, plus heritage.go.kr 국가유산 설명 text loaded from the portal's own ajax file (DATA1/heritage/hub_img/html/cul_*.html). UNESCO register pages for all four items verified via Internet Archive (registration years 1997/2001/2007/2011 with exact wording); Uigwe nomination PDF re-extracted and quotes/section numbers verified; Seungjeongwon nomination PDF could not be re-fetched (captcha) so the author's saved text was used, with other sources backing each fact. Corrections this pass: poswae schedule mistranslation (격 2년 = every third year, not every other year), 'dried herbs' removed, ep5 f4 quote exactified, 3 vocab words not appearing in scenes removed, ep5 f8 second source (정병모 판화사적 연구) and ep6 f3 festival official site added, UNESCO locators replaced by exact page wording, ep3 f7 3,045+198 clarification.

authorNotes: The Analects line: the Korean portal and Encyclopedia texts say '세 가지 기준' ('three standards'), Legge translates Analects 1.4 as 'on three points', and the Encyclopedia also glosses 日三省吾身 as 'three times a day'; because translations differ, the number is DROPPED from narration and the claim, and the Korean quotes in the sources are kept as printed. 'Why?' now says 'One reason': the Encyclopedia also records other readings (the word 省 may echo Yeongjo's 어제자성편; a political motive is also suggested). Naming: 한국민족문화대백과사전 says the final decision on the title cannot be confirmed (in 1781 others proposed 일성록 or 월계록, and Jeongjo objected only to the combined 일월통편), so 'Jeongjo named it' was REMOVED; the story says only that the title is 일성록 and UNESCO translates it as 'Records of Daily Reflections'. The 1783 transition and 'state business grew' are supported by the portal's Korean description and by the Encyclopedia (quoting Jeongjo's 군서표기 in the 홍재전서). The post-accession diary claim (f3) is supported by the portal and by the Encyclopedia ('정조의 일기는 즉위 후에도 계속되었는데'). The Chinese- and Japanese-language machine-translated portal descriptions were removed as sources (f6, f7). 'Every five days' and the 1776 accession year appear only in the portal text and are not in narration. UNESCO page wording is paraphrased (unesco.org unreachable for re-quoting). Framing 'Hoya opens an old book' keeps the story from presenting an imagined meeting with Jeongjo as fact. Omitted: 21 months of missing records; Jeongjo's father's story (tragic).
